---
title: "Inflation fell first, unemployment rose later: The U.S. experience through 2024"
description: "Most of the fall in inflation came before the clearer rise in unemployment."
author: "Yipin Zhang"
date: 2026-10-01
date-modified: 2026-10-06
categories: [inflation, unemployment, data visualization]
image: results/figures/path.png
execute:
  freeze: false

---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
here::i_am("posts/inflation-unemployment/index.qmd")
POST_DIR <- here::here("posts", "inflation-unemployment")
a <- readRDS(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/analysis.rds"))
f <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
date_label <- function(x) format(x, "%B %Y")
qval <- function(label, variable) a$quarterly[[variable]][a$quarterly$label == label]
point <- function(date, variable) a$monthly[[variable]][a$monthly$date == as.Date(date)]
provenance <- read.csv(file.path(POST_DIR, "data/raw/provenance.csv"))
```

In 2022, bringing inflation down raised an uncomfortable question. Would relief at the checkout come at the cost of more people losing work? [Some prominent economists warned of a substantial rise in unemployment](https://www.minneapolisfed.org/article/2022/us-job-matching-holds-up-keeping-a-soft-landing-in-sight), while others thought inflation could ease without a painful recession. For households already struggling with rising bills, the possibility of losing a paycheck made the stakes especially high.

Did unemployment rise throughout the fall in inflation, or mainly later? I focus on mid-2022 through 2024, the two and a half years after the inflation peak.

One reason to expect a tradeoff is that strong spending can encourage hiring while also pushing prices up. Slowing spending could ease price pressure but weaken hiring. This is one idea behind the Phillips curve.

Inflation measures how much prices increased compared with the same month a year earlier. The unemployment rate counts people without a job who are available and actively looking for work, as a percentage of everyone working or looking for work. Falling inflation means prices rise more slowly, not that prices fall.

The first chart shows why timing matters. Inflation peaked at `r f(a$peak$inflation)`% in `r date_label(a$peak$date)` and fell sharply afterward. By December 2024, unemployment had risen `r f(a$end$UNRATE - a$peak$UNRATE)` percentage points from peak inflation, or `r f(a$end$UNRATE - a$trough$UNRATE)` points from its later low.

```{r}
#| label: fig-timeline
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Inflation began falling before unemployment began its sustained rise."
#| fig-alt: "Inflation peaks in June 2022, while unemployment reaches its subsequent low in April 2023 before rising."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/figures/timeline.png"))
```

In July 2024, unemployment had risen enough to trigger the [Sahm rule](https://www.stlouisfed.org/on-the-economy/2025/may/making-sense-recession-probabilities), a widely watched recession warning. Yet [no recession followed through the end of 2024](https://www.nber.org/research/business-cycle-dating). The warning called for caution, but did not mean the soft landing had failed.

Was this simply a predictable exchange between inflation and jobs? The second chart checks whether similar unemployment consistently came with similar inflation. Each point represents one month, grouped into 2015 through 2019 before COVID, the disruption in 2020 and 2021, and the inflation and cooling period from 2022 through 2024.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Months with similar unemployment had very different inflation rates across the three periods."
#| fig-alt: "A scatterplot shows different inflation rates at similar unemployment levels across the three calendar periods."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/figures/scatter.png"))
```

Unemployment was `r f(point("2019-12-01", "UNRATE"))`% in December 2019 and `r f(point("2022-06-01", "UNRATE"))`% in June 2022. Yet inflation was `r f(point("2019-12-01", "inflation"))`% in the first month and `r f(point("2022-06-01", "inflation"))`% in the second. Similar unemployment accompanied very different inflation. Unemployment alone does not explain the price pressures households faced.

How could inflation fall without a collapse in hiring? In his [August 2024 Jackson Hole speech](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/powell20240823a.htm), Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell described strong spending colliding with disrupted supply chains, followed by energy price shocks after Russia invaded Ukraine. He argued that easing those disruptions helped bring inflation down alongside slower demand. The [headline consumer price index includes energy](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/questions-and-answers.htm), so those price swings also affect the inflation measure used here.

The final chart shows how that adjustment unfolded over time. Each point averages three months to make the path easier to follow. Moving downward means inflation fell; moving right means unemployment rose. The chart zooms in on the smaller unemployment changes.

```{r}
#| label: fig-path
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The arrows trace an early fall in inflation followed by a clearer rise in unemployment."
#| fig-alt: "A quarterly path shows substantial initial inflation declines with little unemployment movement, followed by rising unemployment and smaller further inflation declines."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/figures/path.png"))
```

Much of the initial movement was downward. From `r a$start_q$label` to `r a$split_q$label`, inflation fell from `r f(a$start_q$inflation)`% to `r f(a$split_q$inflation)`%, while unemployment stayed close to `r f(a$split_q$unemployment)`%.

Afterward, the path moved more clearly to the right. By 2024 Q4, unemployment averaged `r f(qval("2024 Q4", "unemployment"))`% and inflation `r f(qval("2024 Q4", "inflation"))`%.

Through the end of 2024, this pattern was closer to the soft landing view than to predictions that bringing inflation down would require a large, sustained rise in joblessness. Most of the inflation decline arrived before the clearer unemployment increase. The later warning signal qualifies that favorable outcome rather than erasing it.

These charts cannot establish which policies or supply changes caused the outcome, and small movements in survey estimates should not be treated as exact population changes. The conclusion applies to this period and these national averages, not to every household or what happened after 2024.

The main takeaways are:

* Much of the fall in inflation came before the clearer rise in unemployment.
* The experience through 2024 was closer to a soft landing, but the later unemployment rise was a meaningful warning.
* Similar unemployment came with very different inflation, so unemployment alone does not explain price pressure.

Data come from BLS via FRED's [consumer price index](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CPIAUCSL) and [unemployment rate](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/UNRATE). The [GitHub repository](https://github.com/yipin-grena/aeds6400-blog/tree/main/posts/inflation-unemployment) contains the data, code, methods, and instructions for reproducing the analysis.
